newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Despite setbacks, Argentina to pursue Falklands.
newsitem.headline: Despite setbacks, Argentina to pursue Falklands.

text.p: The Argentine government acknowledged it has given up hope that Britain will yield control of the Falklands through direct talks but vowed to continue its diplomatic "policy of seduction" to win control of the islands.

After a top level meeting in Britain failed to make progress on Argentina 's sovereignty claims, senior officials in Buenos Aires expressed optimism that relations would continue to improve in other areas.

"I believe, and I am very optimistic, that we will head toward the normalization of relations in all areas, except one -- sovereignty," Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella said in an interview with La Nacion newspaper published on Sunday.
"I think we will reach a form of plateau, in which there will be a cordial relation between all sides and there will be disagreement on this point."

Argentina and Britain fought a brief but bloody war over the remote South Atlantic islands in 1982 in which about 1,000 soldiers, mostly Argentine, died. Argentina lost the war but maintains its claim to the islands, which it says were "usurped" by Britain in 1833.

Since Peronist President Carlos Menem came to power in 1989 he has resumed diplomatic ties, hosted visits by British royals and forged close trade links, while insisting he will win back the islands, known as the Malvinas in Argentina, by 2000.

Di Tella has received flak for his "policy of seduction" that has included sending islanders Christmas cards, books and videos. But he claims he has secured a radical change in attitude among the islanders and managed to make the British nervous.
He also said a deal with Britain on oil exploration in the South Atlantic signed last year was "the biggest advance in 170 years" of territorial dispute.

"The policy of seduction has not failed," Menem told reporters on Sunday. "We will press our claim in all international forums. Argentina never stopped making our claim, nor will we stop making our claim to sovereignty over a territory that belongs to it."
Argentina will recover sovereignty "through that other form of war, which is diplomacy," Menem added.

The president seemed to vent frustration at the lack of progress when he said in late December he would be willing to share sovereignty. But London immediately made it clear there was no prospect of shared rule.

Di Tella made a surprise trip to London earlier this month for talks with Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind. While the two agreed to meet in coming weeks over disputed fishing rights in South Atlantic waters, Rifkind would not yield on sovereignty.
The Argentine foreign minister suggested that the Conservatives in Britain are eager to show strength on this and other issues in the run-up to the elections there later this year.
"But rest assured that 60, 90 days after the new government assumes power I will be knocking on the door, asking for a meeting," Di Tella said.
